title: Artificial Intelligence Acquisitions: Agencies Should Collect and Apply Lessons Learned to Improve Future Procurements
author: U.S. Government Accountability Office

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.an: The EntityClusterSummary contains no title, description, key points, or quotations, so there is insufficient evidence to assess the source’s position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: AI procurement: Deployed outcomes outrank adoption counts
st.an: GAO accepts the cluster’s lifecycle-governance proposition and materially develops it with evidence from federal acquisitions: continuing evaluation, tailored contractual and data-rights protections, lifecycle-cost scrutiny, and systematic capture of procurement lessons. It also qualifies the proposition by stressing that its sample is nongeneralizable and no acquisition approach is yet universally superior.
qs: OMB M-25-22 states that agencies should test proposed AI solutions to understand their capabilities and limitations before awarding contracts and should be able to regularly monitor and evaluate an AI system throughout its acquisition life cycle.[fn49] OMB M-25-22 also states that agencies should use data they have defined for validation and testing when conducting any independent evaluations.

Specifically, GAO is recommending that DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA update their policies to require officials to systematically collect lessons learned from AI acquisitions to enable sharing and application by other agencies.

st.t: Federal procurement: Acquisition speed can weaken accountability
st.an: GAO accepts the cluster’s core warning that faster acquisition can weaken post-award safeguards and lifecycle accountability. It materially develops that proposition with case-based evidence on testing, data rights, costs and expertise, plus a concrete recommendation that agencies systematically collect and share procurement lessons; it also cautions that no procurement approach has yet proved superior.

Specifically, GAO is recommending that DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA update their policies to require officials to systematically collect lessons learned from AI acquisitions to enable sharing and application by other agencies.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: GAO accepts the need for selective, context-specific AI deployment and materially extends it into procurement practice: agencies need specialist expertise, adaptable requirements, staged contracting, continuous evaluation, life-cycle cost controls and systematic institutional learning rather than one-time tool acquisition.

kp.k: Audit examines diverse acquisitions, not a representative sample
kp.d: GAO's federal procurement findings derive from a nongeneralizable sample of 13 AI acquisitions at DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA, covering 44 contracts and agreements awarded between September 2018 and February 2025. Commerce was included primarily for government-wide initiatives. The audit ran from October 2024 to April 2026; the six challenge areas were verified across all five selected agencies. These are cross-domain procurement findings, not findings about legal services.
qs: We selected a nongeneralizable sample of 13 AI acquisitions from DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA for in-depth review
From our sample of AI acquisitions, we analyzed 44 contracts and agreements awarded between September 2018 and February 2025 and supporting program documentation.
We then verified that these challenges were issues across all five of our selected agencies.

kp.k: AI adoption expands, but procurement success remains uncertain
kp.d: Citing the Federal Chief Information Officer, GAO reports that federal AI use more than doubled from 2023 to 2024. Selected agencies described new capabilities and potential service efficiencies, including disaster assessment, veterans' benefits analysis, and administrative chatbots. GAO does not establish which acquisition approaches deliver superior outcomes or returns amid rapidly changing technologies, markets, and policies.
qs: According to the Federal Chief Information Officer, federal agencies more than doubled their use of AI from 2023 to 2024

However, in a landscape with rapidly evolving AI capabilities, markets, and federal policy, it is too soon to tell which approaches will most successfully meet agencies’ requirements under different circumstances, and which initiatives will provide the best return on investment.

kp.k: Industry leadership shapes government dependence on commercial capabilities
kp.d: GAO cites Stanford's AI Index for industry producing nearly 90 percent of notable models in 2024 versus 60 percent in 2023, corporate AI investment exceeding $250 billion in 2024, and total investment growing more than thirteenfold since 2014. Agencies procure models, infrastructure, and systems from private companies, while rapid technological change creates uncertainty about durable vendors and capabilities.
qs: The Stanford University Institute for Human-Centered AI reported that the private sector leads AI development, with nearly 90 percent of notable models—those deemed as particularly influential models within the AI ecosystem—originating from industry in 2024 compared to 60 percent in 2023.
Those researchers also found that corporate AI investment reached over $250 billion in 2024 alone.

kp.k: Vendor-driven adoption trades speed for contractual protection
kp.d: GAO distinguishes deliberate agency-directed procurement from vendors introducing AI without specific AI requirements. For example, GSA's maintenance software vendor added a chatbot outside a defined requirement. Agency-directed planning can establish tailored safeguards but delay adoption; vendor-driven upgrades can arrive faster while leaving agencies exposed to unforeseen costs and declining model reliability.
qs: GSA officials told us that the vendor offered the chatbot as an added capability and not in response to a defined requirement.

The benefits of an agency-directed approach using typical acquisition planning steps include a deliberate decision-making process that involves AI terms and conditions that reflect agency requirements.

However, not including AI terms and conditions when using this approach may increase the risk of experiencing unanticipated cost growth and operational challenges, such as “model drift”— decreasing reliability over time.

kp.k: Flexible agreements can weaken accountability and transparency
kp.d: Agencies used both FAR-based contracts and alternative authorities. In July 2025, DOD awarded OTAs with $200 million ceilings to four leading AI companies. GAO describes flexibility concerning IP, award times, and accounting requirements as potential benefits for attracting nontraditional contractors, but cites earlier findings of reduced accountability and transparency. OMB guidance calls for particular transparency and documentation for high-impact AI uses.
qs: In July 2025, DOD awarded OTAs with $200 million ceilings to four leading AI companies to accelerate adoption of advanced AI capabilities across the department.
However, we previously found that agencies’ use of OTAs carries the risk of reduced accountability and transparency compared to FAR-based contracts.
OMB M-25-22 states that agencies may need more transparency rather than less in contracts for AI systems that support “high-impact” use cases.

kp.k: Established contracts accelerate buying but may constrain customization
kp.d: GAO contrasts custom contracts for specific mission requirements with established government-wide vehicles that streamline purchasing. GSA's OneGov strategy and DOD's Tradewinds seek wider access to emerging technologies. However, FEMA officials reported that using an existing contract to meet deadlines limited AI-specific terms and prevented requiring post-award testing of hazard mitigation planning features.
qs: According to OMB guidance, the custom approach is suitable when mission needs are specific and require a high level of agency involvement during contract performance.
OMB guidance states that a key benefit of leveraging established contracts is increased efficiency.
As a result, they told us they could not require the vendor to perform post-award testing to improve hazard mitigation planning features under the existing contract terms.

kp.k: AI procurement frequently centers on continuing services
kp.d: Most reviewed contracts and agreements procured services, often through software-as-a-service licenses. GAO links this approach to ongoing assessment needs and reports that officials managing sophisticated systems considered vendor service quality more consequential for performance than core algorithms. GAO concludes that acquiring AI as a service can often be preferable, rather than identifying a universally superior procurement model.
qs: most of the contracts and agreements we assessed as part of our in-depth reviews were for services.

Additionally, agency officials who manage some of the most sophisticated AI solutions in our sample asserted that the quality of services vendors provide affects performance outcomes more than the quality of model algorithms (i.e., the core software product).
For these reasons, we found that acquiring AI as a service can often be a preferred approach.

kp.k: Technical expertise becomes essential throughout procurement
kp.d: Officials at all five selected agencies identified limited access to specialists as a procurement challenge. Data scientists, software engineers, and cybersecurity experts help define requirements, assess proposals, establish metrics, and oversee performance. VA officials linked expertise shortages to difficulty establishing source-selection criteria; DHS officials reported acquisition delays. OMB directs cross-functional teams incorporating acquisition, technical, legal, privacy, civil rights, budgeting, and other relevant expertise.
qs: Officials from each of our five selected agencies told us that limited access to subject matter experts, such as data scientists and software engineers, was a challenge for procuring AI technologies.
Some of these officials asserted that subject matter experts are critical for defining requirements, such as data and infrastructure needs, and evaluating vendor proposals.
As a result, they reported encountering delays in completing acquisition tasks.

kp.k: Data rights affect operational usefulness and future competition
kp.d: Every selected agency reported difficulty establishing data ownership and IP rights. FEMA officials could not share damage-assessment outputs with federal and state partners because necessary rights had not been obtained at award. Maven officials struggled to define rights sufficient for future competition and still wanted training after a two-day multidisciplinary summit. OMB calls for explicit ownership terms and revisiting agency processes, with standardization where possible.
qs: Officials from each of our five selected agencies identified establishing data ownership and IP rights as a challenge to acquiring AI.

Officials from the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Geospatial Damage Assessment solution told us they could not share model outputs with other federal and state partners because they did not obtain certain data rights at the award phase.
However, following this summit, those officials expressed a continuing need for additional training on IP rights clauses for AI contracts.

kp.k: Traditional acquisition cycles lag rapid AI development
kp.d: Officials at all five agencies described conventional procurement timing and approaches as poorly aligned with AI. Project Linchpin officials rejected a five-year development-then-maintenance model as unsuitable; VA leaders said FAR-based awards can take two years, with approval processes taking up to a year. OMB encourages performance-based techniques that specify objectives and outcomes rather than restrictive traditional statements of work.
qs: Officials from each of our five selected agencies identified traditional acquisition time frames and approaches as poorly aligned with the speed of AI development.
Officials from the Army’s Project Linchpin explained that the traditional approach of developing a system for 5 years, followed by operations and maintenance, does not reflect the realities of AI.
They added that, at this pace, agencies are no longer purchasing innovation.

kp.k: Clear requirements enable enforceable AI performance accountability
kp.d: All five agencies identified requirements definition and contractual terms as challenges. Maven officials reported that early procurement prioritized speed without well-documented requirements, preventing accountability for weekly Agile deliverables; subsequent contracts added metrics and model-performance requirements. VA officials described standard security language as inadequate for protecting veterans' information and sought more comprehensive terms and government-wide contractual language.
qs: These officials learned that without clear requirements defined in contracts they could not hold vendors accountable for weekly deliverables needed for Agile development.
As a result, they are now adding metrics and model performance requirements before awarding follow-on contracts to better evaluate what vendors deliver against user needs.
Specifically, officials reported that VA’s standard security language was not sufficient for the program’s requirements for protecting veterans’ information in a rapidly changing environment.

kp.k: Continuous testing addresses changing performance and value
kp.d: Officials across all five agencies reported difficulty selecting testing methods before and after award. NIST officials attributed the absence of universal tests to heterogeneous, complex AI services. GSA's USAi team described repeated performance testing to assess whether new model versions justify higher prices. OMB advises testing before award, ongoing monitoring, and independent evaluations using representative agency-defined data unavailable to vendors.
qs: For example, NIST officials stated that well-defined, universal AI tests do not exist yet because of the variation and complexity of AI services.
They added that such testing is critical to be able to determine if new versions of those models justify their often much higher prices.
Specifically, the data should not be accessible to the vendor and should be as similar as possible to the data used when the system is deployed.

kp.k: Licensing and infrastructure complicate sustainable AI economics
kp.d: Officials at all five agencies reported uncertainty about AI prices and costs. Army XM-30 officials rejected a proposal of around $300,000 per vehicle per year, which would have exceeded $500 million annually in licensing alone. Project Linchpin officials said buyers underestimate lifecycle costs by considering model training but overlooking ongoing infrastructure, cloud, and compute needs. OMB recommends pricing transparency and lifecycle value assessments incorporating effectiveness and operation and maintenance costs.
qs: These officials also cited uncertainty related to how vendors price AI-related licenses and services.
That proposal would have resulted in more than $500 million each year just for licensing fees in addition to the cost to acquire the vehicles.

Additionally, officials supporting the Army’s Project Linchpin explained that government buyers often underestimate overall costs because they only consider the cost to train AI models and overlook the infrastructure needed to support AI capabilities over time.

kp.k: Experienced programs illustrate adaptable procurement practices
kp.d: GAO presents Maven and USAi practices as potentially transferable lessons, not proven best approaches. Maven reported cross-functional teams, increasingly specific data and performance terms, 90-day sprints, small initial vendor-testing contracts, and comprehensive cost estimation. USAi reported reusing effective contractual terms, pre-award reliability tests, and pursuing usage-based rather than license-based pricing because extensive employee use was not expected.
qs: Maven officials reported awarding relatively small contracts to several AI vendors to test their solutions prior to committing to larger acquisitions.
GSA officials reported reusing contract terms for USAi that were effective in previous AI acquisitions, for example contractual frameworks defining service expectations.

GSA officials reported pursuing a usage pricing model for USAi rather than a licensing approach to reduce overall costs, explaining that most employees are not expected to use the capability extensively.

kp.d: VA retired SoKAT in January 2023 without entering production because its incremental benefits did not justify additional costs, but officials did not document lessons despite other suicide-prevention acquisitions. FEMA likewise failed to document observed dwelling-classification problems or anticipated regional accuracy issues. Although the main text describes a further 12-month vendor period, Appendix I records DHS's February 2026 report that both Geospatial Damage Assessments and Planning Assistance for Resilient Communities had been retired.
qs: For example, VA officials told us they decided to retire the SoKAT solution, which supported suicide prevention efforts, in January 2023, after officials determined that it did not improve upon existing solutions enough to justify the additional cost.
Specifically, they did not document that they found the AI model struggled to distinguish between different types of dwellings.
In February 2026, DHS officials reported this effort has been retired and is no longer in use at FEMA.

kp.k: GAO recommends mandatory collection and sharing of lessons
kp.d: GAO confirmed that DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA policies lacked formal processes or requirements for systematically documenting AI acquisition lessons; senior leaders confirmed this for policies effective as of September 2025. OMB expected policy updates by December 29, 2025 and knowledge sharing through a GSA repository. GAO issued one recommendation to each agency to establish collection processes and submit lessons, including contract-clause practices, to that repository. All four concurred; DHS planned guidance updates by July 2026. Concurrence and plans do not establish completed implementation.
qs: Our review of the four agencies’ departmental AI policies confirmed that none of the policies include a formal requirement or process to consistently document lessons learned even though some articulate their value.
We are making a total of four recommendations: one to DOD, one to DHS, one to GSA, and one to VA.
DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA concurred with our four recommendations and identified plans to address them in responses reproduced in appendices II – V.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: This cross-domain source claims that expanding federal AI adoption creates opportunities for new capabilities and faster services, but requires procurement practices adapted to evolving models, recurring costs, data rights, and continuous performance assessment.
pts.d:
1. Adoption and service delivery: GAO reports, citing the Federal Chief Information Officer, that federal agencies more than doubled AI use between 2023 and 2024. Officials at the five selected agencies say AI can supply previously unavailable capabilities or deliver services more efficiently. Examples include disaster-damage assessment, veterans’ claims analysis, military imagery analysis, and administrative chatbots. These are capability and intended-benefit claims, not quantified findings of productivity improvement.
2. Procurement trade-offs: GAO says deliberate, agency-directed procurement can establish appropriate AI terms but delay adoption; vendor-driven upgrades can arrive faster but risk cost growth and operational problems when AI-specific protections are missing. Established contracts can accelerate acquisition, whereas custom procurement can better accommodate particular mission needs. Non-FAR agreements can offer flexibility and attract nontraditional vendors, but GAO cites reduced accountability and transparency risks.
3. Services rather than one-time products: GAO finds acquiring AI as a service can often be preferable because ongoing assessment is needed. Officials managing some sophisticated systems assert that vendor service quality affects outcomes more than model algorithms do.
4. Expertise and contract design: Officials across all five agencies identify technical-expertise shortages, data and IP protections, procurement timing, requirements and contract terms, testing, and costs as challenges. GAO presents examples in which insufficient expertise delayed acquisition work, inadequate data rights prevented sharing outputs, and vague requirements impeded vendor accountability. Army and VA officials argue traditional multiyear development and award cycles are poorly aligned with AI’s pace of change.
5. Reliability: Officials across the five agencies say diverse, complex AI systems require early and continuous testing. NIST officials say universal, well-defined AI tests do not yet exist. GSA officials say repeated testing is needed both to track performance and to determine whether more expensive model versions justify their prices.
6. Economics: Army Project Linchpin officials say buyers underestimate total costs when they count model training but omit supporting infrastructure and future computing needs. GAO warns acquired capabilities may consequently become too expensive to sustain. GSA officials describe USAi usage-based and complexity-sensitive pricing as intended to reduce unnecessary expenditure, not as demonstrated savings.
7. Learning from procurement: GAO finds DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA were not systematically collecting acquisition lessons because agency policies lacked requirements and processes. GAO concludes that this raises the risk of repeating avoidable, costly mistakes and recommends mandatory collection and sharing. All four agencies concurred.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: GAO combines a nongeneralizable procurement case sample, contract and policy review, interviews, external adoption statistics, and prior audit findings; many benefits and risks are attributed to officials rather than independently measured.
pts.d:
The audit reviewed 13 AI acquisitions at DOD, DHS, GSA, and VA, analyzing 44 contracts and agreements. It also interviewed senior acquisition leaders and program officials, reviewed departmental policies, and analyzed OMB guidance; Commerce’s contribution centered on government-wide initiatives rather than sampled acquisitions. GAO selected six challenge areas from interviews and confirmed they arose across all five agencies. The adoption-growth statistic comes from the Federal CIO’s account of the 2024 use-case inventory, not GAO’s sample.
Concrete cases support the procurement claims: FEMA officials reported being unable to share damage-assessment outputs because required data rights had not been obtained; Maven officials reported that insufficient contractual requirements prevented accountability for weekly deliverables; FEMA planning officials said an existing contract enabled faster procurement but could not require post-award testing. Army XM-30 officials described rejecting a proposal costing about $300,000 per vehicle annually, over $500 million annually across the fleet in licensing alone; these are proposed, rejected costs, not expenditures. VA officials said SoKAT was retired because its improvement over existing solutions did not justify its additional cost. FEMA officials reported observed difficulty distinguishing dwelling types, while anticipating—not demonstrating—accuracy problems in different regions. GAO’s policy review corroborated the absence of formal lesson-collection requirements. Prior GAO audits support claims about OTA transparency risks and acquisition-management problems. The report offers no general causal estimate of efficiency gains, savings from knowledge sharing, or comparative superiority of procurement approaches.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report describes adoption and procurement experience through 2025 within an October 2024–April 2026 audit; future benefits remain conditional, and GAO expressly says it is too early to identify the most successful approaches.
pts.d:
The report is dated April 13, 2026. Adoption growth concerns 2023–2024; the detailed contract sample spans September 2018–February 2025, with some strategic initiatives and acquisition approaches examined through fiscal year 2025. The finding that departmental policies did not require systematic lesson collection was confirmed as of September 2025. OMB issued M-25-22 in April 2025 and directed policy updates by December 29, 2025; agency concurrence is not evidence that implementation was complete. DHS planned guidance updates by July 2026.
Benefits depend on procurement circumstances: custom acquisitions suit specific mission needs and intensive agency involvement; established vehicles can accelerate standardized purchases; vendor-driven additions risk gaps when AI terms are absent. Continuous assessment is framed as necessary throughout deployment, especially for high-impact uses. Future savings from usage pricing depend on GSA’s expectation that most employees will not use the capability extensively. GAO does not establish a universal best acquisition model or a return-on-investment forecast.
Program status qualifies examples: SoKAT was retired in January 2023 without entering production. Although the narrative discusses continuing FEMA damage-assessment procurement and potential future uses, Appendix I records DHS’s February 2026 report that both Geospatial Damage Assessments and Planning Assistance for Resilient Communities had been retired. They should therefore be treated as acquisition experiences, not necessarily current deployments.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected parties are government buyers, AI suppliers, technical and legal procurement personnel, mission users, and members of the public whose services or interests depend on AI-supported decisions.
pts.d:
Federal acquisition officials and program managers face new requirements for technical collaboration, lifecycle costing, contractual protections, testing, and knowledge sharing. Data scientists, software engineers, cybersecurity personnel, privacy specialists, legal advisers, and other experts contribute to requirements, vendor selection, rights allocation, and ongoing oversight; the source does not predict legal-job displacement or changes to law-firm markets. Vendors encounter differing opportunities and obligations depending on procurement vehicles, transparency requirements, licensing models, and data-rights terms. Government-wide vehicles and platforms are intended to make commercial models more readily available to agency staff.
Operational beneficiaries and risk bearers include veterans and their families receiving benefits and health services, communities seeking disaster recovery or hazard planning support, airport travelers subject to facial comparison, and military personnel using imagery and targeting assistance. Other federal and state partners can lose access to useful outputs when rights are inadequate. High-impact uses receive special attention because AI output may principally inform decisions affecting civil rights, safety, or other significant interests. These public-service consequences are distinct from claims about access to civil legal assistance, which the report does not make.
